assignments.text:
But Peter did not come back. That spring day was the last time he ever saw his
mother’s face. The writer of the letter—the last—the only person
who had ever seen what was written in it, was dead long ago; and I, a stranger,
not born at the time when this occurrence took place, was the one to open it.
assignments.summary: Peter never received the mother's letter and never saw her again; the letter remained unopened and lost for years until Mary Smith opens it in the present.

assignments.text:
“Elegant economy!” How naturally one falls back into the phraseology of

“vulgar and ostentatious”; a sort of sour-grapeism which made us very peaceful
and satisfied.
assignments.summary: The narrator reflects on how Cranford inverses values: economy becomes elegant and spending becomes vulgar, a sour-grape philosophy that creates social peace.
assignments.best_quote: 'Elegant economy!' How naturally one falls back into the phraseology of Cranford!

assignments.summary: Miss Matty confesses that in quiet moments, she imagines hearing Peter's footsteps approaching, her heart quickens, but the sound always fades—Peter never returns.
assignments.best_quote: And then again, when I sit by myself, and all the house is still, I think I hear his step coming up the street, and my heart begins to flutter and beat; but the sound always goes past—and Peter never comes.

assignments.text:
It is so long ago, and no one
ever knew how much I thought of it at the time, unless, indeed, my dear mother
guessed; but I may say that there was a time when I did not think I should have
been only Miss Matty Jenkyns all my life; for even if I did meet with any one
who wished to marry me now (and, as Miss Pole says, one is never too safe), I
could not take him—I hope he would not take it too much to heart, but I
could  not  take him—or any one but the person I once thought I
should be married to; and he is dead and gone, and he never knew how it all
came about that I said ‘No,’ when I had thought many and many a
time—Well, it’s no matter what I thought.

assignments.text:
It was full of love, and sorrow, and pride in his new profession, and a sore
sense of his disgrace in the eyes of the people at Cranford; but ending with a
passionate entreaty that she would come and see him before he left the Mersey:

assignments.summary: Peter's letter to his mother expresses love, sorrow for his disgrace, and pride in his naval profession, ending with a passionate plea to see her before possible battle.

assignments.text:
He was a half-pay captain, and had obtained some situation on a
neighbouring railroad, which had been vehemently petitioned against by the
little town; and if, in addition to his masculine gender, and his connection
with the obnoxious railroad, he was so brazen as to talk of being
poor—why, then, indeed, he must be sent to Coventry. Death was as true
and as common as poverty; yet people never spoke about that, loud out in the
streets.
assignments.summary: Captain Brown's poverty confession is doubly offensive because he is a man connected to the disliked railway; poverty is a taboo subject like death.
assignments.best_quote: Death was as true and as common as poverty; yet people never spoke about that, loud out in the streets.

assignments.text:
My father
saw no conscious look in his wife’s hot, dreary eyes, and he missed the
sympathy that she had always been ready to give him—strong man as he was,
and at the dumb despair in her face his tears began to flow. But when she saw
this, a gentle sorrow came over her countenance, and she said, ‘Dearest John!
don’t cry; come with me, and we’ll find him,’ almost as cheerfully as if she
knew where he was.
assignments.summary: When the mother sees her husband's tears, she overcomes her own despair and gently leads him onward with renewed hope and tenderness.
assignments.best_quote: But when she saw this, a gentle sorrow came over her countenance, and she said, 'Dearest John! don't cry; come with me, and we'll find him,' almost as cheerfully as if she knew where he was.

assignments.text:
There were letters of stilted penitence to his father, for
some wrong-doing; and among them all was a badly-written, badly-sealed,
badly-directed, blotted note:—“My dear, dear, dear, dearest mother, I
will be a better boy; I will, indeed; but don’t, please, be ill for me; I am
not worth it; but I will be good, darling mother.”
assignments.summary: Among the scrape letters is a badly written, blotted note from Peter to his mother, begging forgiveness and pleading her not to fall ill on his account.
assignments.best_quote: My dear, dear, dear, dearest mother, I will be a better boy; I will, indeed; but don't, please, be ill for me; I am not worth it; but I will be good, darling mother.

assignments.text:
“My dear, that boy’s trick, on that sunny day, when all seemed going straight
and well, broke my mother’s heart, and changed my father for life. It did,
indeed. Old Clare said, Peter looked as white as my father; and stood as still
as a statue to be flogged; and my father struck hard! When my father stopped to
take breath, Peter said, ‘Have you done enough, sir?’ quite hoarsely, and still
standing quite quiet.
assignments.summary: Peter bears the flogging in stoic silence; old Clare witnesses his white face and unflinching posture, and reveals that this shocking public incident broke the mother's heart and permanently changed the father.
assignments.best_quote: 'Have you done enough, sir?' quite hoarsely, and still standing quite quiet.

assignments.text:
“Oh, gentility!” thought I, “can you endure this last
shock?” For Miss Barker had ordered (nay, I doubt not, prepared, although she
did say, “Why, Peggy, what have you brought us?” and looked pleasantly
surprised at the unexpected pleasure) all sorts of good things for
supper—scalloped oysters, potted lobsters, jelly, a dish called “little
Cupids” (which was in great favour with the Cranford ladies, although too
expensive to be given, except on solemn and state occasions—macaroons
sopped in brandy, I should have called it, if I had not known its more refined
and classical name).
assignments.summary: A second tray arrives with supper: scalloped oysters, potted lobsters, jelly, and 'little Cupids' (macaroons sopped in brandy), sumptuous fare that tests genteel propriety.
assignments.best_quote: Oh, gentility! thought I, can you endure this last shock?

assignments.text:

the profits of brown soap and moist sugar enabled the proprietor to go straight
to (Paris, he said, until he found his customers too patriotic and John Bullish
to wear what the Mounseers wore) London, where, as he often told his customers,

assignments.text:
Old gowns, white and

with miniatures of ladies and gentlemen sweetly smiling out of a nest of stiff

fashion of the day—the ladies of Cranford always dressed with chaste
elegance and propriety, as Miss Barker once prettily expressed it.

evening, as we sat over the fire, in which she evidently looked upon a husband
as a great protector against thieves, burglars, and ghosts; and said that she
did not think that she should dare to be always warning young people against
matrimony, as Miss Pole did continually; to be sure, marriage was a risk, as
she saw, now she had had some experience; but she remembered the time when she
had looked forward to being married as much as any one.

“And my father, my dear, dear father! I will not complain now, if God will give
me strength to be patient. But, oh, Jessie! tell my father how I longed and
yearned to see him at last, and to ask his forgiveness. He can never know now
how I loved him—oh! if I might but tell him, before I die! What a life of
sorrow his has been, and I have done so little to cheer him!”

A light came into Miss Jessie’s face. “Would it comfort you, dearest, to think
that he does know?—would it comfort you, love, to know that his cares,
his sorrows”—Her voice quivered, but she steadied it into
calmness—“Mary! he has gone before you to the place where the weary are
at rest. He knows now how you loved him.”
assignments.summary: Miss Jessie gently tells her sister that their father is already dead and in heaven, where he now knows how much she loved him.

Instead of tying up preserves in the
store-room, however, we went to talk in the dining-room; and there Miss Jenkyns
told me what Major Gordon had told her; how he had served in the same regiment
with Captain Brown, and had become acquainted with Miss Jessie, then a
sweet-looking, blooming girl of eighteen; how the acquaintance had grown into
love on his part, though it had been some years before he had spoken; how, on
becoming possessed, through the will of an uncle, of a good estate in Scotland,
he had offered and been refused, though with so much agitation and evident
distress that he was sure she was not indifferent to him; and how he had
discovered that the obstacle was the fell disease which was, even then, too
surely threatening her sister.
assignments.summary: Miss Jenkyns explains that Major Gordon served with Captain Brown and fell in love with Miss Jessie when she was young; he proposed when he inherited a Scottish estate but was refused because of her sister's illness.

It was only,

My father was amongst them, meaning, he said, to ask them to walk
into the garden with him, and admire the beautiful vegetable production,
when—oh, my dear, I tremble to think of it—he looked through the
rails himself, and saw—I don’t know what he thought he saw, but old Clare
told me his face went quite grey-white with anger, and his eyes blazed out
under his frowning black brows; and he spoke out—oh, so
terribly!—and bade them all stop where they were—not one of them to
go, not one of them to stir a step; and, swift as light, he was in at the
garden door, and down the Filbert walk, and seized hold of poor Peter, and tore
his clothes off his back—bonnet, shawl, gown, and all—and threw the
pillow among the people over the railings: and then he was very, very angry
indeed, and before all the people he lifted up his cane and flogged Peter!
assignments.summary: The Rector sees through the rails and is seized with rage; he orders the crowd to stay, rushes into the garden, strips Peter of his disguise, and brutally canes him before all the assembled townspeople.
